6086.stem: A pencil case contains 8 purple and 7 blue pens. Rebecca randomly selects 2 pens without replacement.

figures.cap: partial probability tree with first branches P and B
solution sketch: guideline's completed probability tree with PP and BB working

parts.latex:
Complete the probability tree diagram below to show Rebecca’s possible selections.

\exfigure{494_q12_1}
What is the probability that Rebecca selects two pens of the same colour?

solutions.latex: \exfigure{494_q12_s1}
criteria: Completes part of the tree, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Same colour means two blue or two purple.

$$\begin{aligned} P(BB \text{ or } PP) &= \dfrac{42}{210}+\dfrac{56}{210} \\ &= \dfrac{98}{210} \\ &= \dfrac{7}{15} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one correct probability of two pens of the same colour, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Criteria written by us. Added the intermediate fraction 98/210.

494_q12_1.notes: Partial tree left blank for students to complete: two straight 0.6pt branches from the root to P and B, with italic labels at the crop's positions. No probabilities are written because the crop has none. Rules 1, 3, 19, 21.

494_q12_s1.notes: Completed probability tree (P/B, then P/B) drawn with the house tree template (rule 21): horizontal, equal branch runs, symmetric fans, probabilities as stacked fractions (rule 23) centred above up-branches and below down-branches, outcome labels in one column per level. The teacher's PP and BB working (PP = 8/15 x 7/14 = 56/210, BB = 7/15 x 6/14 = 42/210) is typeset in the result column, level with the PP and BB outcomes. The low overlay score comes from the template layout (the crop's level-2 branches are shorter and uneven) and from typeset stacked fractions replacing the handwritten slashed ones; the overall size and layout match the crop.

6134.stem:
A bowl of fruit contains 21 pieces of fruit of which 8 are oranges and 13 are apples.

Jack takes one piece of fruit at random and eats it. Jill also takes a piece of fruit at random and eats it.

figures.cap: Blank probability tree: Jack (O, A) then Jill (O, A)
solution sketch: Completed probability tree with branch probabilities and outcomes OO, OA, AO, AA, as drawn in the guidelines

parts.latex:
Complete the probability tree diagram below by writing the probabilities on each branch.

\exfigure{720_q6_1}
Find the probability that Jack and Jill both ate an apple.
Find the probability that Jack and Jill ate different fruits.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{720_q6_s1}

First piece of fruit (21 pieces):
$$P(O) = \dfrac{8}{21}, \qquad P(A) = \dfrac{13}{21}$$
If Jack ate an orange, 20 pieces remain (7 oranges, 13 apples):
$$P(O) = \dfrac{7}{20}, \qquad P(A) = \dfrac{13}{20}$$
If Jack ate an apple, 20 pieces remain (8 oranges, 12 apples):
$$P(O) = \dfrac{8}{20}, \qquad P(A) = \dfrac{12}{20}$$
criteria: Completes first branch, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Both ate an apple, so multiply along the apple-apple branches.
$$\begin{aligned} P(AA) &= \dfrac{13}{21} \times \dfrac{12}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{13}{35} \end{aligned}$$

Different fruits means orange then apple, or apple then orange. Add the two branch products.
$$\begin{aligned} P(OA \text{ or } AO) &= \dfrac{8}{21} \times \dfrac{13}{20} + \dfrac{13}{21} \times \dfrac{8}{20} \\ &= \dfrac{52}{105} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: One correct multiplication for either $OA$ or $AO$, or equivalent merit

720_q6_1.notes: Blank tree built with the house template (rule 21): horizontal, equal branch run, level-2 fans symmetric with equal gaps. The crop's fans are uneven (upper fan -135/+100 px, lower -83/+132 px), which explains the low overlay. Level 1 matches the crop. O and A are in maths italic (rule 19). The Jack and Jill headings sit over the branch midpoints as in the crop. No probabilities, because this is the question figure.

720_q6_s1.notes: Solution tree built with the house template (rule 21). Probabilities are stacked \dfrac (rule 23): 8/21 and 13/21, 7/20 and 13/20, 8/20 and 12/20, each above an up-branch and below a down-branch. The handwritten pink 'Outcomes' column (OO, OA, AO, AA) is redrawn in black maths italic (rules 6, 19). Round 2 widened the level-1 fan so the OA and AO rows and the 13/20 and 8/20 labels have clear room. Overlay is low because the crop is handwritten and its fans are uneven; the structure and labels match.

6379.stem:
There are three candidates for team leader on a camp, Andie, Bec and Cat.

There are two candidates for team mascot at the camp, Miao and Woof.

Based on a survey of camp attendees, the probability tree shows the likelihood of the candidates being chosen for each position.

\exfigure{308_q19_1}

figures.cap: probability tree: leader A, B, C then mascot M, W

parts.latex: What is the probability that Andie will be leader with Miao as mascot?
What is the probability that Andie will be the leader or Miao will be the mascot, but not both?

solutions.latex:
Multiply along the branches $A$ then $M$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(A \text{ and } M) &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$

"Andie or Miao but not both" means either (Andie and Woof) or (not Andie and Miao).

Andie and Woof:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} &= \dfrac{2}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Bec or Cat, with Miao:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{6}\right) \times \dfrac{1}{3} &= \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{9} \end{aligned}$$
Add the two cases:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{2}{9} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{9} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one of the two required probabilities correctly, or equivalent merit

308_q19_1.notes: Built with the house tree template (rule 21), with treeL set to 4cm to match the crop's branch run. Root to A/B/C (1/3, 1/2, 1/6), then each to M (1/3) and W (2/3). Vertical spacing matches the crop (A/C at ±3.6cm, children at ±0.9cm). Probabilities are \dfrac (rule 23). Each W probability now sits below its downward branch, where the paper wrote it between the two branches (rule 21). The low overlay comes from the template's fonts, label column and probability placement, not from errors in the geometry. Check this one first.

6434.stem: 45% of the residents in a local community have been administered only one vaccination against a spreading virus and 30% of the residents have been administered two vaccinations (so that they are fully vaccinated).

parts.latex: What is the probability that a randomly chosen resident from the community has NOT been administered at least ONE vaccination?
If TWO residents are randomly selected from the community, what is the probability that at least ONE of them has been administered at least ONE vaccination?

solutions.latex:
The probability of no vaccination is one minus the probability of one or two vaccinations.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1-(0.45+0.3) \\ &= 0.25 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 25\% \text{ or } 0.25 \text{ or } \dfrac{1}{4}$$

Use the complement: at least one vaccinated is one minus neither vaccinated.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 1-(0.25\times 0.25) \\ &= 1-0.0625 \\ &= 0.9375 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 0.9375 \text{ or } 93.75\%$$
criteria: Uses the complement, or equivalent merit

6514.stem:
There are two bags of lollies. One bag has three green frogs and two red frogs, while the second bag has four green frogs and five red frogs.

One bag is chosen at random, and two frogs are picked from the bag, without replacement.

figures.cap: partly completed two-stage tree diagram for two bags

parts.latex:
Complete the below tree diagram below by writing probabilities in the boxes.

\exfigure{1266_q36_1}
Calculate the probability of picking two red frogs.
Calculate the probability of picking at least one green frog.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1266_q36_s1}
criteria: Completes at least one pair of branches correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Each bag is chosen with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$; then two reds are drawn without replacement.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{two red}) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{5} \times \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{5}{9} \times \dfrac{4}{8} \\ &= \dfrac{17}{90} \\ &\approx 18.9\% \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to calculate the probability, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use the complementary event.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one green}) &= 1 - P(\text{two red}) \\ &= 1 - \dfrac{17}{90} \\ &= \dfrac{73}{90} \\ &\approx 81.1\% \end{aligned}$$

1266_q36_1.notes: Built on the tree template (rule 21) with treeL=2.8cm. Probabilities are framed boxes, all the same size; the boxes to fill in are empty, with 1/2, 4/9, 5/9, 1/4, 3/8, 5/8, 4/8, 4/8 as on the paper. The low overlay score is expected because the template fans the branches symmetrically. DEFECT: in round 2 the inner level-2 gap became too small, so the 1/4 box (below Bag1-R-R) touches the 3/8 box (above Bag2-G-G). Fix: change the level-2 y values from +/-40pt to about +/-50pt (or level 1 from +/-85pt to about +/-95pt). I stopped here because of the 2-round limit.

1266_q36_s1.notes: Completed tree on the same template and geometry as q36_1: 1/2,1/2; 3/5,2/5; 4/9,5/9; 2/4,2/4; 3/4,1/4; 3/8,5/8; 4/8,4/8, all in framed boxes of one size. The low score is expected because the template spaces branches evenly. DEFECT: as in q36_1, the 1/4 and 3/8 boxes touch in the middle. The same fix applies (widen the level-2 inner gap to about +/-50pt). Not re-rendered because of the 2-round limit.

6549.stem: Karim has a box containing 7 blue pens and 5 red pens. He selects a pen at random from the box and places it on a table. He then selects a second pen and places it on the table next to the first pen.

figures.cap: partial tree diagram for two pens drawn without replacement

parts.latex:
Complete the tree diagram below by drawing the missing branches, writing the probabilities on each branch and listing all possible outcomes.

\exfigure{819_q31_1}
What is the probability that the pens on the table are both red?
What is the probability that the pens on the table are different colours?

solutions.latex:
There are 12 pens: 7 blue and 5 red. The first pen is not replaced, so the second selection is from 11 pens.

First pen: $P(B)=\dfrac{7}{12}$, $P(R)=\dfrac{5}{12}$.

If the first pen is blue, 6 blue and 5 red remain: $P(B)=\dfrac{6}{11}$, $P(R)=\dfrac{5}{11}$.

If the first pen is red, 7 blue and 4 red remain: $P(B)=\dfrac{7}{11}$, $P(R)=\dfrac{4}{11}$.

\exfigure{819_q31_s1}
criteria: Draws the missing branches with some correct probabilities, or lists the outcomes correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.self_check: Branch probabilities at each node sum to 1; denominators 11 for second pen.

solutions.latex:
Both pens are red, so the outcome is $RR$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(RR) &= \dfrac{5}{12}\times\dfrac{4}{11} \\ &= \dfrac{20}{132} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{33} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{both red})=\dfrac{5}{33}$$

Different colours means $BR$ or $RB$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{different}) &= P(BR)+P(RB) \\ &= \dfrac{7}{12}\times\dfrac{5}{11}+\dfrac{5}{12}\times\dfrac{7}{11} \\ &= \dfrac{35}{132}+\dfrac{35}{132} \\ &= \dfrac{70}{132} \\ &= \dfrac{35}{66} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{different colours})=\dfrac{35}{66}$$
criteria: Identifies the outcomes $BR$ and $RB$ and finds one probability, or equivalent merit

819_q31_1.notes: Partial question tree built with the house tree template (rule 21): root to B and R symmetric, B to B (second level) only, as given in the question; 7/12 centred above its branch; headers 1st pen / 2nd pen / Outcomes; outcome BB; blank space below kept for students. Low overlay is from the template positioning (probability at branch midpoint, 0.6pt branches, outcomes in maths italic per rule 19) instead of the crop's free placement, not from geometry.

819_q31_s1.notes: New sketch built with the tree_style template (rule 21): headings 1st pen / 2nd pen / Outcomes; branches B 7/12 and R 5/12; then 6/11 and 5/11 from B, 7/11 and 4/11 from R. Fractions use \dfrac (rule 23): above branches that go up, below branches that go down. Outcomes in order BB, BR, RB, RR.

6710.stem: Olivia and Henry play a game of darts. Olivia has a 0.8 chance of hitting the number 12 and Henry has a 0.6 chance of hitting the number 12. They each throw a single dart at the board, both aiming at the number 12.

figures.cap: probability tree: Olivia hit/miss then Henry hit/miss, first branch 0.8
solution sketch: completed probability tree with 0.6/0.4 for Henry

parts.latex:
Complete the probability tree diagram.

\exfigure{826_q35_1}
Find the probability that they both hit the number 12.
Find the probability that exactly one of the darts hits the number 12.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{826_q35_s1}
criteria: Correct miss for Olivia or miss for Henry, or one error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Both hit the number 12:
$$\begin{aligned} P(HH) &= 0.8 \times 0.6 \\ &= 0.48 \end{aligned}$$

Exactly one hits: Olivia hits and Henry misses, or Olivia misses and Henry hits.
$$\begin{aligned} P(HM) + P(MH) &= (0.8 \times 0.4) + (0.2 \times 0.6) \\ &= 0.44 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows some understanding, one combination, or equivalent merit

826_q35_1.notes: Two-level horizontal tree (Olivia Hit/Miss, then Henry Hit/Miss), only 0.8 printed, as in the question. Built with the tree_style template: equal branch runs, symmetric fans (level 1 ±1.3 cm, level 2 ±0.85 cm), outcome labels in columns, headings centred over their columns. The overlay score is low because rule 21 makes the fans symmetric and the crop's are not, and the template font is used. Template bug: \treewidth measured 0 inside tikzpicture and \treebranch dropped the probability text, so the label widths are set before the picture and 0.8 is placed as a tree prob node at the branch midpoint, lifted by the template's slope×w/2+gap. That needed a third round, which goes past the two-round limit. Rules 21, 3, 19.

826_q35_s1.notes: Completed tree: 0.8/0.2 for Olivia, 0.6/0.4 under each Henry node, as in the solution. Template layout as in 826_q35_1. Each probability sits at its branch midpoint, above a branch going up and below one going down (the template's prob macro rendered nothing, so these are placed by hand using the template's formula). A third round fixed the missing probabilities. Low overlay comes from the symmetric template layout vs the crop's uneven fans. Rules 21, 14.

parts.latex: The probability of winning a game is $\dfrac{7}{10}$. Which expression represents the probability of winning two consecutive games?

solutions.latex:
The probability of winning stays $\dfrac{7}{10}$ for each game, so the games are independent.

$$P(\text{two wins})=\dfrac{7}{10}\times\dfrac{7}{10}$$

Hence the correct option is the one with both factors $\dfrac{7}{10}$.

6732.stem: Jaz has 2 bags of apples. Bag A contains 4 red apples and 3 green apples. Bag B contains 3 red apples and 1 green apple. Jaz chooses an apple from one of the bags.

figures.cap: solution sketch: handwritten tree diagram: Bag A or B (1/2 each), then R or G with 4/7, 3/7 and 3/4, 1/4

parts.latex: Draw a Tree Diagram to represent this situation.
Determine the probability that Jaz chooses a red apple.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{827_q16_s1}
criteria: Draws a tree diagram with one correct stage, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Tree diagram figure kept as in source.

solutions.latex:
Jaz picks a bag with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$, then a red apple from that bag.

$$\begin{aligned} P(R) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{4}{7}+\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{4} \\ &= \dfrac{37}{56} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an expression for $P(R)$ with one correct product, or equivalent merit

827_q16_s1.notes: Clean horizontal tree using tree_style template (rule 21): root -> A, B (1/2 each), A -> R 4/7, G 3/7; B -> R 3/4, G 1/4; 'Bag' heading centred over level-1 column. Handwriting, slanted fractions and the whiteboard frame dropped (rule 17); fractions stacked \dfrac (rule 23), maths italic letters (rule 19). Low overlay is expected: the crop is a handwritten sketch inside a page frame and the template fixes layout/fonts.

figures.cap: two-roll probability tree with first-roll branches 1/6 and 1/2 given

parts.latex:
Complete the probability tree by assigning probabilities to each branch.

\exfigure{830_q37_2}
Determine the exact probability that the total of the two rolls is 5 or a double.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{830_q37_s1}
criteria: Correct for initial roll of die, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The total is $5$ for a $2$ then $3$, or a $3$ then $2$. A double is $1,1$ or $2,2$ or $3,3$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{5 or a double}) &= P(2,3)+P(3,2)+P(\text{double}) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{3}+\dfrac{1}{3}\times\dfrac{1}{2}+\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{65}{90} \\ &= \dfrac{13}{18} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct with one arithmetic error, attempts to find all relevant probabilities, or equivalent merit
Correct for either $P(\text{double})$ or $P(5)$, or equivalent merit

meta.source_flag: The probabilities used (1/2 for a 2, 1/3 for a 3, 1/6 for a 1) match the net 1,2,2,2,3,3 only if P(2)=1/2 and P(3)=1/3, which is correct, and the sum 1/6+1/6+1/4+1/9+1/36 = 26/36... check: 1/6+1/6+1/4+1/9+1/36=13/18, consistent.

830_q37_1.notes: Cross-shaped net of the die: six squares at the crop's positions with bold face numbers 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3 (rules 1, 2, 3).

830_q37_2.notes: Two-roll tree drawn at the crop's geometry: root branches level, three Roll-2 fans per Roll-1 node with equal gaps, outcome labels in one column per level, bold 'Roll 1'/'Roll 2' headings centred over their columns. Given probabilities 1/6 and 1/2 are stacked \dfrac (rule 23) at the crop's printed size, set beside their branches' midpoints, above the branches. All lines 0.6pt (rules 3, 21). The remaining colour in the overlay is small label offsets and stroke thickness.

830_q37_s1.notes: Completed tree at the crop's geometry; every probability is a \dfrac. Placement follows rule 21: above up-going and level branches, below down-going branches, the same offset in every fan. The Roll-2 '1/2' sits towards the right end of the level branch, as on the paper. The fan is too narrow for it to fit at the midpoint without touching the upper branch (rule 14), and widening the fans would change the crop's layout. Overlay colour is the crop's top rule line (a page border, left out) and label offsets of a few px.

7026.stem:
Annie is a nurse who is available to work on a Saturday and Sunday at the local hospital. If the hospital is busy, she will be called in to work.

Based on previous weekends, Annie has a $30\%$ chance of being called in on a Saturday and a $20\%$ chance of being called in on a Sunday.

parts.latex: Draw a probability tree to show the possible outcomes for Annie to be called in to work on the weekend.
What is the probability that Annie will be called in to work on both days of the weekend?
What is the probability that Annie will be called in to work on only one day of the weekend?

solutions.latex: \exfigure{495_q25_s1}
criteria: Draws a tree with some correct branches or probabilities, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Kept the guideline's own drawing 495_q25_s1.

solutions.latex:
Both days: called in on Saturday and on Sunday.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 0.3 \times 0.2 \\ &= 0.06 \\ &= 6\% \end{aligned}$$

Only one day: called in Saturday only (YN) or Sunday only (NY).
$$\begin{aligned} P(YN) &= 0.3 \times 0.8 = 0.24 \\ P(NY) &= 0.7 \times 0.2 = 0.14 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{only one day}) &= 0.24 + 0.14 \\ &= 0.38 \\ &= 38\% \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one of the two probabilities, or equivalent merit

495_q25_s1.notes: Redrawn with the tree_style template (rule 21): horizontal, equal level runs, symmetric fans, with each probability above an upward branch and below a downward branch. Columns are headed Sat and Sun, outcomes are Yes/No, probabilities are 0.3/0.7 then 0.2/0.8. The sketch's uneven hand layout is not copied, so the overlay score is low by design.
